messages.author: 159be5dfa13b5981
messages.subject: Bootstrapping Pairwise Procrustes Distances
parts:
Hi, 

So I'm using this paper by Baab [2008] as a reference - and I'd like to compare the empirical distribution of bootstrapped Squared Procrustes Distance (SSD, n = 7) to the SSD of a reference sample. I have code for randomly reproducing samples of size 7:

keep <- c(39:57) 
UM2_hei <- UM2[,, keep]
rm(keep)
data <- aperm(UM2_hei, c(3,2,1))
dim(data)<-c(19,88)
data2<-replicate(999,data[sample(1:nrow(data),size=7,replace=TRUE),],simplify=FALSE)

And I have code for producing all the combinations of shape distances between 2 individuals:

keep <- c(39:57) 
UM2_hei <- UM2[,, keep]
rm(keep) 

UM2_hei <- two.d.array(UM2_hei)
UM2_hei <- matrix(as.numeric(unlist(UM2_hei)), nr=nrow(UM2_hei), nc=ncol(UM2_hei))

UM2_hei_speclist <- tapply(UM2_hei, rep(1:nrow(UM2_hei), ncol(UM2_hei)), function(i)i)

UM2_hei_combn <- combn(1:length(UM2_hei_speclist), 2)

UM2_hei_res <- lapply(as.data.frame(UM2_hei_combn), function(x)do.call(rbind, UM2_hei_speclist[x]))

F1<-function(res){
  Spec1<-as.matrix(res[1,])
  Spec2<-as.matrix(res[2,])
  dim(Spec1)<-c(44,2)
  dim(Spec2)<-c(44,2)
  Shape.Dist<-sin(riemdist(Spec1,Spec2))
}

UM2_hei_asd <- lapply(UM2_hei_res, F1)

heidelbergensis <- (unlist(UM2_hei_asd))
hist(as.numeric(UM2_hei_asd))

However, I am reasonably unexperienced in R, and I can't figure out how to loop this so that it would perform the Procrustes distances calculations with say 1000 sub-samples of size 7 individuals. I was wondering if anyone would be able to help me?

Thanks, 

Seán Lea

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Bootstrapping Pairwise Procrustes Distances
parts:
Seán,

The simplest way to do bootstrap resampling is with the sample function in R, using an important argument, replace = FALSE.

For any array of shapes, there are three dimensions.  For example

dim(A)

produces three numbers in the order of p, k, n.  If you want to sample specimens, try this:

spec.ind <- 1 : (dim(A)[3])
sample(spec.ind, replace = FALSE) # finds a random sampling of 1 to n, with replacement

A[, , sample(spec.ind, replace = FALSE) ] # finds a random sampling of 1 to n, with replacement, and selects their landmarks from A

If you want to sample landmarks, try this

lm.ind <- 1 : (dim(A)[1])
sample(lm.ind, replace = FALSE) # finds a random sampling of 1 to p, with replacement

A[sample(lm.ind, replace = FALSE), , ] # finds a random sampling of 1 to p, with replacement, and selects those points from A

In a loop, one would do something like the following:

SSD <- list()
pers <- 999

for(i in 1:perms) {

# calculate statistics using bootstrap permutations, as above and your math
SSD[[i]] <- stat or c(stat1, stat2, …)
}

I used 999, in case you want to append the observed case to the list to make it 1,000.  Thus,

SSD <- c(obs, SSD)

would do that.

Hope that helps!
Mike

Thanks a lot, Professor Collyer!

I came up with this - it's probably incredibly inefficient - but am I right in thinking that this should function?

keep <- c(39:57) 
UM2_hei <- UM2[,, keep]
rm(keep)

UM2_hei <-unlist(UM2_hei)
UM2_hei <-two.d.array(UM2_hei)
UM2_hei <-arrayspecs(UM2_hei, 44, 2)

data <- aperm(UM2_hei, c(3,2,1))
dim(data)<-c(19,88)

A <- replicate(10000,data[sample(1:nrow(data),size=7,replace=TRUE),],simplify=FALSE)

Z <- list()
B <- list()

for (i in 1:10000) {
  
  spec1 <- as.data.frame(A[[i]])
  spec1 <- matrix(as.numeric(unlist(spec1)), nr=nrow(spec1), nc=ncol(spec1))
  speclist <- tapply(spec1, rep(1:nrow(spec1), ncol(spec1)), function(i)i)
  combn <- combn(1:length(speclist), 2)
  res <- lapply(as.data.frame(combn), function(x)do.call(rbind, speclist[x]))

F1<-function(res){
    Spec1<-as.matrix(res[1,])
    Spec2<-as.matrix(res[2,])
    dim(Spec1)<-c(44,2)
    dim(Spec2)<-c(44,2)
    Shape.Dist<-sin(riemdist(Spec1,Spec2))
    
  }

asd <- lapply(res, F1)
    asd <- (unlist(asd))
    
    Z <- sapply(asd, function(x) x^2)
    B[i] <- Reduce("+", Z)
    
    
}


Seán

parts:
Sean

One other thing I would add on top of what Mike has already suggested is that it may be worth spending a bit of time learning how to use the boot library. While a simple non-parametric bootstrap is very easy to write thanks to indexing and the sample function, there are a few aspects that are incredibly helpful which the boot library makes efficient. In particular the "strata" argument (so you can sample with replacement within each level of a treatment group, i.e. sampling within male observations and within female observations, but keeping their sample sizes the same as in the real data set). Additionally, getting slightly "better" approximations of the confidence intervals (like the bias corrected and accelerated, BCa confidence intervals) is an important plus. These can also be coded by hand, and are not that difficult, but the boot library has been "checked" by many eyes and so there is less chance of little goofy errors.

Also, there are some nice tutorials available for bootstrapping (using R). Keep in mind though that since for each observation your response vector is multidimensional, to sample using the index and not the observations themselves.

A great one is 
https://socialsciences.mcmaster.ca/jfox/Books/Companion/appendix/Appendix-Bootstrapping.pdf

Here is one of my old tutorials. Not a great set, but they may be useful
 https://youtu.be/TP6r5CTd9yM
 https://youtu.be/ydtOTctg5So

Cheers
Ian
